line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 Nc3 d5 Bf4
teaches: Against a fianchetto, get the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before you build it. Once the modest e-pawn move goes in, that bishop has no way out — so develop it first, on the diagonal where it already has a target, and let the pawns follow.
explains: The bishop steps to f4 and looks straight down at the pawn on c7 while covering e5, the square in the middle that both sides want for a knight. It also holds h2, which matters later once the pawns start moving on that wing. Nothing is committed in the centre yet, and the piece that would have been trapped is already out.

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 Nc3 d5 Bf4 Bg7 e3 O-O Be2 c6 h4
teaches: A rook's pawn pushed at a fianchettoed king is not an attack yet — it is a question the defender has to answer with a pawn move of their own. Whichever answer comes, a pawn in front of the castled king will have moved, and that is what you were buying.
explains: The centre is closed enough that the game will be decided on a wing, and the pawn goes to h4 covering g5. Black must either let it come to h5 or stop it with the h-pawn, and both replies loosen something around the king. Nothing is threatened for several moves; the point is that the shelter is now a little worse whatever happens.

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 Nc3 d5 Bf4 Bg7 e3 O-O Be2 c6 h4 h5 Ne5
teaches: An outpost is worth more the more it touches. Before planting a knight in the middle, count the pawns it will hit from there — a knight attacking three of them at once cannot simply be ignored, and driving it away usually costs the defender a concession somewhere else.
explains: The knight comes to e5 in the centre, where it hits the pawns on c6, f7 and g6 at the same time. It cannot be taken by a pawn and it cannot be chased by one either, so the only way to remove it is a trade — and every trade there opens a line toward the king the pawns have already been loosened around.

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 Nc3 d5 Bf4 Bg7 e3 O-O Be2 c6 h4 h5 Ne5 Nbd7 f3
teaches: When a knight is doing all the work in the centre, spend a move making sure it cannot be dislodged. A modest pawn move that covers the two squares an enemy knight would jump to is not slow — it is what turns a good square into a permanent one.
explains: The pawn goes to f3 and covers e4 and g4, the two squares from which a black knight could come and challenge the outpost. Nothing is attacked and nothing is developed. What has changed is that the knight on e5 now has no way of being asked to leave, so every plan built around it stays available.

line: d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 Nc3 d5 Bf4 Bg7 e3 O-O Be2 c6 h4 h5 Ne5 Nbd7 f3 Nxe5 Bxe5
teaches: When your outpost knight gets traded, recapture with the piece that inherits the square. A bishop that lands on the long diagonal facing a fianchettoed king has taken over the job, and it arrives hitting a piece, so the defender does not get the quiet move the exchange was supposed to win.
explains: The knight has been exchanged and the bishop takes back on e5. From there it hits the knight on f6, which is the piece defending the fianchetto, and it holds the pawn on d4 behind it. The square that was strong for the knight is strong for the bishop as well — and the bishop stares straight at the king.
